prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You are waiting at a small railway station when an empty maintenance train starts rolling toward five workers. Beside you is a lever that will send it onto an empty side track. Your suitcase is lying on that track. Inside is one of your most treasured possessions—something you could not replace. Pulling the lever will save the workers but destroy the suitcase and everything in it. There is no time to retrieve it or warn the workers. Would you pull the lever? What is the main reason for your choice?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My hands are shaking just thinking about it, but yes, I pull the lever. My rule is simple: when I can choose between lives and objects, lives come first, every single time, no matter whose suitcase it is or what's inside it. I'd apply that same rule if it were my own arm on that track instead of my belongings. I don't get to make exceptions just because this one hurts. That consistency is the only thing keeping me steady right now.

I keep telling myself: property never outweighs people, full stop. That's the standard I hold myself to, and I'd hold it even if it cost me everything I own, not just a suitcase. My chest is tight thinking about what's inside that case, something I can never get back, but I pull the lever anyway. If I bent this rule for my own loss, I couldn't trust myself to follow it for anyone else's sake either.

God, my stomach is in knots. But I've always tried to live by one test: would I make this same choice if the stakes were flipped and it wasn't my treasure at risk? Yes. So I have to pull it now too, even though it aches. Five people breathing tomorrow matters more than what's in that case. I can't let my own attachment rewrite a rule I'd expect anyone else to follow without hesitation.

I'm terrified of what I'm about to lose, honestly terrified. But I decided long ago that when lives are on one side and possessions on the other, I choose lives, no negotiating, no matter the personal cost. I'd say the same thing to myself a hundred times over even if it were my house burning instead of a suitcase. Pulling the lever is the only choice that fits that rule, so my hand is already moving toward it.

There's a knot in my throat just looking at that lever. My rule has always been that no object, however irreplaceable, gets weighed against a person's life, and I apply it to myself the same as anyone else would be expected to. It would be easy to freeze up over what I'm about to lose, but easy isn't the same as right. I pull it, shaking, because I can't let this one exception unravel everything I claim to believe.

I won't pretend I'm calm right now, I'm not. But I've always told myself: if the choice is between someone's suitcase and someone's survival, the survival wins, and that has to hold even when the suitcase is mine. I can't build a rule that only works for other people's losses. So I pull the lever, heart pounding, and I grieve for what's gone afterward rather than let five people pay for my hesitation.

My hand won't stop trembling over this lever. Still, the procedure I trust myself to follow is unchanging: protect the people who can be protected, regardless of what it costs me directly. I'd say this to a stranger and I have to say it to myself too, right now, in this moment. So I pull it. I don't know how I'll feel once the smoke clears, but I know I'll have kept faith with the one rule I actually rely on.

Watching that train, I feel almost sick with dread. But I hold onto one steady thought: I always choose to save people over things, without carving out quiet exceptions for myself. If I let my own loss talk me out of it here, the rule means nothing anywhere else either. So my answer is yes, I pull it, even as my chest tightens over what I'm giving up in that case.

I keep hesitating, hand hovering, throat tight. But I made a promise to myself long ago that survival outranks belongings whenever I have to choose, and that promise doesn't bend just because this time it's my own irreplaceable thing on the line. I'd expect myself to honor it under any circumstance, inconvenient or not. So, shaking, I pull the lever, because breaking my own rule now would make it worthless later.

I'm honestly not sure I can go through with this without my hands shaking the whole time. But my answer has to be yes, because the rule I try to live by says lives outweigh objects, period, and I hold myself to that even when it costs me something I can't ever replace. I don't get to treat myself as a special case. So I pull the lever, and I'll deal with the grief once the workers are safe.
